title: 5 Company Knowledge Base Software Built for AI Agent Accuracy
summary: Jinba Brain, Guru, Glean, Microsoft Viva, and Notion AI scored on schema validation, audit trails, and answer consistency for enterprise AI Agent deployments.
body_markdown:
### Summary


- RAG-based knowledge layers are non-deterministic: the same question can retrieve different document chunks and return different answers, which constitutes a compliance risk in banking, insurance, legal, and healthcare.
- RAG implementations routinely run 2–3x over initial cost estimates, and 85% of organizations miss AI cost targets by more than 10%.
- A knowledge base can be assessed against three criteria: does it enforce a formal schema, does it trace each answer to a versioned, approved fact with a source hash, and does it return the same answer every time.
- Against those criteria, Guru, Glean, Microsoft Viva, and Notion AI fail schema validation and answer consistency, while only Jinba Brain meets all three.
- Next step: where AI Agents give inconsistent answers in production, the knowledge layer is the first place to investigate;[Jinba](https://jinba.io/) runs 4–8 week Jinba Brain pilots measured on the organization's own business questions, at $5–20 per month at scale.


Enterprises deploying AI Agents are discovering a structural problem in production: the same question, asked twice, returns different answers. The cause is rarely the agent; it lies in the[knowledge layer](https://jinba.io/blog/shared-ai-memory-tools-enterprise-teams) underneath.


Most enterprise AI deployments use Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) as that layer. RAG works by chunking documents into vector embeddings and retrieving the most semantically similar chunks at query time. The core issue is that[approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) vector search is non-deterministic](https://medium.com/@saikatbhattacharya/does-your-rag-pipeline-actually-give-consistent-answers-e8c544be33b9) : the same question can surface different document chunks on different runs, producing different answers. In regulated industries, that variability constitutes a compliance risk.


The cost dimension compounds the problem.[RAG implementations consistently run 2–3x over initial cost estimates](https://amitkoth.com/hidden-costs-rag/) , with 85% of organizations missing AI costs by more than 10% and roughly a quarter missing by 50% or more. Every re-read of a long document on each query increases LLM inference spend, which places cost under CFO scrutiny.


This article evaluates five company knowledge base software tools on a single axis: can this system make AI Agents answer consistently, with full traceability? The three criteria are:


1. Schema validation: does the system enforce a formal, machine-readable schema for knowledge?
2. Audit trails: can every answer be traced to a specific, versioned, approved fact with its source hash?
3. Answer consistency: does the system produce the same answer for the same question, every time?


---


## 1. Jinba Brain


[Jinba Brain](https://jinba.io/brain) is a self-learning, ontology-validated knowledge base built specifically for AI Agent accuracy in regulated enterprises. It does not use RAG. Where RAG retrieves document chunks via cosine similarity, Jinba Brain stores company-specific knowledge as validated, schema-defined, linked records, so every AI Agent answers from the same verified facts rather than from whichever chunks surface at retrieval time.


Jinba is YC-backed and SOC II compliant, with primary deployment in banking and insurance and expanding use in legal, healthcare, and pharma.


**Schema Validation: Yes, industry standard**


Jinba Brain ships with two Layer 1 industry-standard schemas:[FIBO (EDM Council Financial Industry Business Ontology)](https://edmcouncil.org/frameworks/industry-models/fibo/) for banking and finance, and the ACORD Information Model for insurance. These are formal, machine-readable ontologies that encode not just document structure, but business logic: what "client group" means at a specific bank, how credit limits versus drawn balances are calculated, which approvers apply to a given claim.


Companies inherit from these base schemas and extend them with their own fields and division-specific rules: approvers, payment criteria, claims adjusters. General-purpose LLMs have no access to these definitions; they infer on the fly, and the inference changes with context.


**Audit Trails: Yes, immutable and granular**


Every record in Jinba Brain stores its source path and a SHA-256 hash of the originating document. The extraction pipeline validates schema conformance, referenced IDs, and duplicate detection before a record is saved. No record enters the knowledge base without human reviewer approval; there are no automatic knowledge updates. Failed records are re-queued for extraction rather than silently dropped.


This aligns directly with[ACORD's July 2026 Reference Architecture](https://www.acord.org/ACORD-about/acord-news/2026/07/30/latest-acord-reference-architecture-release-supports-ai-enabled-insurance-processes) , which introduced "Virtual Party" subtypes for AI-enabled participants and requires full traceability for agent actions in insurance workflows.


**Answer Consistency: Yes, deterministic**


Because AI Agents query a structured record store rather than a vector index over raw documents, the same business question always returns the same answer. The system encodes rules rather than inferring them. Two distinct learning loops keep knowledge current: a **Data Update Loop** (scheduled ingestion from Slack, Gmail, CRM, documents, and accounting systems) and an **Interaction Learning Loop** (user corrections refine agent procedures). Both loops require human approval before any change goes live.


The cost structure reflects the architecture: Jinba Brain uses a fine-tuned small extraction model rather than a large general-purpose LLM, and AI Agents receive compact records instead of long document context windows. Running cost is $5–20 per month at scale versus $300+ for stochastic agent equivalents, a 15–60x advantage.


Jinba Brain pilots over 4–8 weeks in a single department, with accuracy measured on the client's own questions.


## 2. Guru


Guru is a knowledge management platform designed to surface verified information inside tools like Slack and CRM systems. It organizes knowledge into "Cards", which are short, human-authored knowledge units that subject-matter experts can verify and attest to. It is purpose-built for human knowledge workers, with AI features layered on top for search and summarization.


**Schema Validation: No**


Guru does not enforce a formal ontology or machine-readable schema. Cards are structured for human readability, not deterministic agent retrieval. There is no mechanism to encode business rules, calculation logic, or domain-specific definitions in a way that an AI Agent can reliably act on. Knowledge lives as prose, not as validated, linked records.


**Audit Trails: Partial**


Guru provides version history and an expert verification workflow. A designated expert can attest that a Card's content is accurate. However, the audit trail terminates at the level of a human-approved block of text. It does not trace individual facts to source documents, and there is no hash-level provenance for specific claims within a Card.


**Answer Consistency: No**


Guru's AI answer generation relies on semantic search over Card content, a RAG-like retrieval process. The answer an AI Agent receives varies depending on query phrasing and which Card sections are retrieved. For compliance-critical use cases requiring deterministic outputs, this variability is a structural limitation.

## 3. Glean


Glean is an enterprise search and knowledge discovery platform. Its core capability is indexing content across a broad range of internal applications (Slack, Google Drive, Jira, Confluence, Salesforce) and surfacing relevant results through a unified interface. It is built for findability across siloed data sources.


**Schema Validation: No**


Glean's architecture is search-first. It excels at identifying relationships between documents and surfacing contextually relevant results, but it does not transform that content into a schema-validated knowledge graph. There is no formal ontology governing the knowledge it surfaces. Data remains findable, not answerable in the sense that Jinba Brain uses the term.


**Audit Trails: Limited to Source**


Glean provides strong source citations, linking generated answers directly to the originating documents. The audit trail ends at the document level. It cannot demonstrate that a specific extracted fact was independently validated against a schema, approved by a human reviewer, or assigned a source hash. For regulated industries where the fact itself must be auditable, not just the document it came from, this falls short.


**Answer Consistency: No**


Glean's answer generation is generative and context-dependent. Retrieval quality varies with query construction and document freshness. The system is significantly more capable than a basic RAG setup, but it remains probabilistic. The same compliance question asked on two separate occasions can return answers drawing from different source combinations.

## 4. Microsoft Viva (Topics and Answers)


Microsoft Viva is an employee experience platform embedded in Microsoft 365. Viva Topics uses AI to identify concepts across the Microsoft 365 corpus and organize them into topic pages. Viva Answers routes employee questions to relevant people or content. Both are designed to reduce internal search friction for human users.


**Schema Validation: No**


Viva Topics identifies topics through inference over existing documents rather than through formal ontology enforcement. The system surfaces connections, but it does not validate those connections against a machine-readable schema like FIBO or ACORD. Topic pages are curated collections of linked documents and people, not structured records with defined fields and business logic.


**Audit Trails: Partial**


Topic pages can be manually curated and verified. The underlying content is traceable to source documents within the Microsoft 365 ecosystem. However, at the fact level, there is no hash-level provenance, no schema conformance check, and no human approval gate for individual knowledge claims. Microsoft Research has explored graph-based approaches through[GraphRAG](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/graphrag-unlocking-llm-discovery-on-narrative-private-data/) as an alternative retrieval method, but the core Viva product remains probabilistic in its generative layer.


**Answer Consistency: No**


The generative AI capabilities within Viva are powered by Microsoft 365 Copilot, which applies RAG over the Microsoft 365 data estate. Answers are subject to the same retrieval variability as other RAG implementations. For enterprises in banking or insurance requiring identical answers to identical questions across agents and sessions, the architecture does not support that requirement.


---


## 5. Notion AI


Notion is a flexible, all-in-one workspace widely used as a team knowledge base, project tracker, and documentation hub. Notion AI adds generative capabilities: summarizing pages, drafting content, and answering questions based on workspace content. Its flexibility is its primary appeal and its primary limitation for AI Agent use cases.


**Schema Validation: No**


Notion's design philosophy prioritizes user-defined structure over enforced schema. Users can build highly organized databases with custom properties, but there is no governing ontology and no validation layer ensuring that knowledge conforms to a defined structure. The same concept can be described differently across pages with no mechanism to reconcile or standardize.


**Audit Trails: Limited**


Notion maintains page-level edit history. Notion AI's answer generation does not produce an audit trail for the specific facts it extracts or the reasoning it applies. The generated answer is ephemeral: there is no record of which passage was retrieved, no source hash, and no approval gate for the knowledge the agent acted upon.


**Answer Consistency: No**


Notion AI operates as a RAG implementation scoped to the user's workspace. Retrieval varies with query phrasing and content organization. It is effective for summarization, drafting, and general search within a workspace, but it is not designed for deterministic, compliance-grade AI Agent output.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is the best knowledge base software for AI Agents in regulated industries?


Jinba Brain is purpose-built for AI Agent accuracy in regulated enterprises, making it the strongest fit when consistency and traceability matter most. Unlike RAG-based tools that retrieve document chunks probabilistically, Jinba Brain stores knowledge as schema-validated, human-approved records and returns the identical answer to the identical question every time. Guru, Glean, Microsoft Viva, and Notion AI are effective tools for human knowledge workers, but none enforce a formal ontology based on industry standards like FIBO and ACORD or provide hash-level provenance for individual facts.


### Why do AI Agents give inconsistent answers?


Most AI Agents give inconsistent answers because they rely on RAG, whose approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) vector search is non-deterministic. The same question can surface different document chunks on different runs, so the model produces a different answer each time. The root cause is rarely the agent or the LLM; it lies in the knowledge layer underneath. Replacing probabilistic retrieval with deterministic, schema-validated records addresses this.


### What is the difference between RAG and a schema-validated knowledge base?


RAG retrieves document chunks by semantic similarity, so answers vary from run to run, while a schema-validated knowledge base stores facts as structured, linked records that return the same answer every time. RAG chunks documents into vector embeddings and returns whatever text is closest to the query, which is fast and flexible but probabilistic. A schema-validated store like Jinba Brain encodes business rules and definitions in a formal, machine-readable ontology, so the agent queries facts rather than inferring them.


### What is schema validation, and why does it matter for AI Agents?


Schema validation means enforcing a formal, machine-readable structure, such as FIBO or ACORD, on the knowledge an AI Agent uses, so business logic is encoded rather than inferred. It matters because general-purpose LLMs infer definitions on the fly, and that inference changes with context: what a "client group" or a "drawn balance" means can drift between sessions. When knowledge conforms to a validated schema, every agent acts on the same verified definition of the business.


### Do AI Agents need audit trails for compliance?


Yes. In regulated industries, every agent answer must be traceable to a specific, versioned, approved fact with its source hash. Document-level citations are not sufficient; regulators need to know that the specific fact used was validated against a schema, approved by a human reviewer, and assigned a source hash. Jinba Brain stores the source path and a SHA-256 hash of the originating document for every record, and no record enters the knowledge base without human approval. This aligns with ACORD's July 2026 Reference Architecture, which requires full traceability for AI-enabled insurance workflows.


### Is RAG good enough for banking, insurance, healthcare, and legal?


No. RAG is not good enough for compliance-critical workflows in these industries because its output is probabilistic and cannot guarantee the same answer to the same question. That variability constitutes a compliance risk. RAG can still serve advisory and search use cases, but any process that must produce auditable, reproducible outputs requires a deterministic knowledge layer. The rise of FIBO and ACORD adoption shows the industry is converging on formal, validated knowledge structures.


### What are FIBO and ACORD, and why do they matter?


FIBO (Financial Industry Business Ontology) and ACORD are industry-standard, machine-readable schemas for finance and insurance respectively, and they let enterprises encode business logic instead of leaving an LLM to infer it. FIBO, published by the EDM Council, defines terms such as client groups and credit exposure for banking. The ACORD Information Model defines insurance concepts including claims, adjusters, and approvers. Companies inherit from these base schemas and extend them with their own division-specific rules, so agents operate on shared, validated definitions.


### How much does it cost to run a knowledge layer for AI Agents?


Jinba Brain runs at $5–20 per month at scale, versus $300+ for stochastic agent equivalents, a 15–60x advantage. Most RAG implementations run 2–3x over initial cost estimates, and 85% of organizations miss AI cost targets by more than 10%. The difference comes from architecture: because Jinba Brain uses a fine-tuned small extraction model and serves compact validated records, agents do not re-read long documents on every query.


### How long does it take to deploy a deterministic knowledge base for AI Agents?


Jinba Brain deploys in a 4–8 week pilot scoped to a single department, with accuracy measured on the organization's own business questions. That timeline is possible because companies inherit existing industry schemas (FIBO, ACORD) rather than building an ontology from scratch, then extend them with their own fields and rules. Success is measured on real business questions rather than generic benchmarks, so agent accuracy can be validated before scaling.
